description:
Almost dark when I saw something flash from under my office window and scoot under one of the nearby Cleveland Sage bushes. All that remained showing was the tip of a white tail as it flicked back and forth. There were some quail on the other side of the bush but they were wary and flew off. I quickly grabbed my camera Seconds later this fellow crawled back out from under the sage. Just a brief pause to show by his expression that he was disappointed to have missed his dinner opportunity and he was gone.

Our bobcats have been saved by the recent ban on bobcat trapping in California. It used to be a fairly regular and joyful opportunity to see them. Bobcat trapping due to the increase in demand for the fur trade in countries like China devastated the population. With the ban in place we have hope for recovery in the near future. Seeing one of these beautiful creatures is such a privilege.

description: Longest piece is about 4-5”. It lay atop the duff of a trail on the bluff above a creek (location is changed by several miles to protect this mezopredator). Would not have thought feline but for reading that bobcats mark den areas by leaving scat unburied. Can a scatologist lend a hand about this observation?

I arrived at the preserve and walked up to the ledge overlooking the majority of the preserve, including the riparian forest and some of the meadows around it.  As I scanned the area below, I noticed a bobcat walking at the edge of a small meadow.  It stopped and began looking for prey, and mere seconds later had locked on to something (see the fourth pic wear it is sitting and concentrating intently).  Then it crouched down, wiggled its backside, and pounced.  I couldn't see what it ended up with, but it took whatever it caught and disappeared out of view behind some grass to eat it.  The bobcat then reappeared for a moment, looking around the meadow, before retreating back down into the dried up river bed behind it.  The whole experience lasted only about five minutes (I checked the time on the photos to be sure), but it seemed to last much longer.  Amazing to see a skilled hunter do what it does best and secure another meal.

description: We saw a beautiful bobcat in our front yard in Thousand Oaks (near Hillcrest and Conejo School Road).  It was on Sunday 3/10 at 6:30 PM.  The bobcat was walking down our long driveway (we live on a flag lot next to a large open space).  My daughters heard our driveway motion sensor go off and they looked out our front window.  They were so excited and said "Mom, Dad, there's a REALLY BIG CAT in our front yard!!)  We raced over to the window and saw the bobcat.  He was gorgeous and he had a tracking collar around his neck.  I found out later when I talked to Joanne Moriarty, that it was "Bobcat B363."  She told me they caught him after the November fires and he weighed 22 lbs.  He squeezed through our metal fencing and went to our HOA park where he sat down in front of a large tree.  He basically camoflauged himself.  At that point, we went outside to take a closer look at him.  We stared at him through the gate and he stared right back at us.  We stayed far enough away to not be a threat to him or for him to be a threat to us.  We were so excited to be in his presence!  We had our cell phones with us so we took photos but it was dusk and the photo quality is not good.  I'm sharing the pictures anyway but I wish we were able to get better images.  We were in awe of that beautiful creature and we hope he was able to find whatever food he was looking for (there are bunnies and squirrels everywhere).  We hope to see him again sometime.  It was a magical experience for us and I'm happy to take part in any studies about bobcats.  I think they are fabulous!!!

Bobcat was walking along trail, turned into Toyon and Interior Live Oak brush and fallen dead limbs.  It was then sitting about 20 ft from me and looking up into brush at sparrows.  It sat for four or five minutes then came back to trail, walked along it for 30 ft then turned off into broken thicket of limbs and a fallen tree.  I played dying squirrel predator call and it came back toward me, sat, and waited another 5-10 min. watching  me with curiosity until I finally left.  Body size was much larger than domestic cat, perhaps 25 lbs., mottled brown, tan, white pelage, black edged and pointed ears, and while it walked away from me, very clearly seen and unmistakeable was a distinct very short (3-5in.?) tail that was upturned and all white beneath.
